summary: Audited both files against fetched EPA sources. Summer file has an unsourced, mathematically broken table; needs Quick Answer with specific numbers. Winter file delivers 5 of 8 promised causes; needs restructuring or scope trimming. Both require source-layering. Full claim ledger and required edits detailed below.
findings: Summer file (1,280w): No Quick Answer with numbered causes exists — only a descriptive paragraph. Needs replacement with top-3 causes (outdoor watering, tiered pricing, hidden leaks) each with sourced numbers.

Summer file table 'Summer Water Usage Breakdown' contains 6 rows of unsourced per-activity gallon estimates. The 'Total difference' of +85-115 gal/day does NOT match the sum of the individual row differences (~285 gal/day max). This is both unsourced AND mathematically incorrect — must be deleted or replaced with verified data.

Summer file makes irrigation/evaporation claims in prose (h3 #3 'Pools, hot tubs, and water features') that are directionally correct but carry no inline citations. EPA Start Saving page confirms pool covers reduce evaporation; EPA Outdoors page confirms 30% of household use is outdoor. These claims can be kept if sourced with these EPA references.

Winter file (846w): Title promises '8 Common Causes' but body delivers only 5: (1) longer billing cycle, (2) indoor leaks, (3) more hot water use, (4) sewer averaging changes, (5) estimated reads. Must either add 3 more winter-specific causes (e.g., freeze-thaw pipe bursts, seasonal rate adjustments, holiday guest impact) or retitle to '5 Common Causes'.

Winter file has existing sources frontmatter pointing to watersense-current and watersense-current-winter-2024 — both fetched successfully and relevant. The newsletter pages confirm winter is a good time to check for leaks (12k gal/month threshold for family-of-4). The inline [1][2] citations match the sources footer.

Winter file's 'Short answer' (Quick Answer equivalent) lists 4 causes but no specific numbers. Per the mission, top 2-3 causes should have sourced numbers: EPA fixaleak page provides 9,300+ gal/yr leak waste and 10% bill savings from fixes.

Summer file has ZERO sources in frontmatter and ZERO inline citations. Winter file has sources but uses generic seasonal newsletter URLs — neither URL contains the specific data claimed in the body (e.g., longer billing cycle, sewer averaging math).

EPA pages all fetched successfully and confirmed current (retrieved 2026-08-29): How We Use Water, Start Saving, Fix a Leak Week, Outdoors, WaterSense Current newsletters. All share the same WaterSense brand and are consistent.
evidence: EPA How We Use Water page (https://www.epa.gov/watersense/how-we-use-water, retrieved 2026-08-29): 'Nationally, outdoor water use accounts for 30 percent of household use yet can be much higher in drier parts of the country.' and 'The average American family uses more than 300 gallons of water per day at home. Roughly 70 percent of this use occurs indoors.'

EPA Start Saving page (https://www.epa.gov/watersense/start-saving, retrieved 2026-08-29): 'Of the estimated 29 billion gallons of water used daily by households in the US, nearly 9 billion gallons, or 30 percent, is devoted to outdoor water use. In the hot summer months, or in dry climates, a household's outdoor water use can be as high as 70 percent.' and 'The average family spends $1,300 per year in water costs, but can save $500 from retrofitting with WaterSense labeled fixtures and ENERGY STAR® certified appliances.'

EPA Fix a Leak Week page (https://www.epa.gov/watersense/fixaleak, retrieved 2026-08-29): 'The average household's leaks can account for more than 9,300 gallons of water wasted every year' and 'Fixing easily corrected household water leaks can save homeowners about 10 percent on their water bills.' Also: 'If a family of four exceeds 12,000 gallons per month [in winter], there could be serious leaks.'

EPA Outdoors page (https://www.epa.gov/watersense/outdoor, retrieved 2026-08-29): 'Residential outdoor water use across the United States accounts for nearly 8 billion gallons of water each day, mainly for landscape irrigation.'

Current summer file content (content/blog/why-is-my-water-bill-higher-in-summer.md): 1,280 words, no Quick Answer with numbered causes, an unsourced table with broken arithmetic, 0 sources in frontmatter or body.

Current winter file content (content/blog/why-is-my-water-bill-higher-in-winter.md): 846 words, 5 causes delivered vs 8 promised in title, existing but generic source URLs, frontmatter sources match body citations.

Model sibling content/blog/25-utility-bill-taxes-fees-franchise-charges-explained.md: shows the expected pattern — action-first Quick Answer with bolded key takeaway, verified-examples table with per-row source citations, sources footer.

test_results: none (read-only audit, no file modifications made)
risks: Summer table with broken arithmetic ('Total difference: +85-115 gal/day') does not match sum of row differences (~200-290) — if published as-is, a sharp reader will flag it and the site loses credibility with the audience it's trying to earn (evidence-seeking, bill-stressed homeowners).

Winter file's '8 Common Causes' promise sets an expectation the body doesn't meet. A reader counting causes will find 5 and feel misled — especially one who came from the summer '7 Common Causes' article and expects symmetry.

Both files lack the Quick Answer pattern the site has adopted for standard pages. The Quick Answer is the first thing users see and the primary SEO rich-snippet target — omitting the numbered-lead format hurts both user comprehension and search visibility.

Summer file has 0 sources total — every number in the table and every claim about billing, leaks, and usage is unverifiable. This is exactly the pattern that triggered AdSense's 'Low value content' rejection. A single audit of the site would flag this file immediately.

Winter file sources point to generic EPA newsletter pages rather than pages with the specific data the article references. The EPA 'How We Use Water' page and 'Fix a Leak Week' page contain the actual hard numbers the article needs but doesn't cite.
unknowns: Source of the summer table's arbitrary per-activity gallon estimates (50-200 gal/day for lawn, 10-30 for pool, etc.) — not found at any EPA page fetched. These may be from a non-EPA source, a tool like the WaterSense calculator, or invented.
Whether the winter file originally had 8 planned causes that were cut during drafting, or if '8 Common Causes' was chosen for SEO keyword density without corresponding body sections.
Whether the author intentionally left summer file with 0 sources (expecting a future pass) or considered the prose general knowledge not requiring citations.
Whether winter data about 'sewer averaging' resets in winter is accurate for most US utilities — the article cites no source for the claim that utilities 'reset sewer averages during winter months.'
recommendation: Both files need a structured human edit pass before publication. Priority order: (1) Fix summer table — either delete it entirely and replace with the EPA 30%/300-gal/day/9,300-gal-leak framework, or source every row to an EPA or AWWA publication. (2) Add the Quick Answer to both files using the verified-examples pattern: bold lead sentence + numbered top-2/3 causes with sourced numbers. (3) Choose and execute on the winter file's scope mismatch — either add 3 more causes (freeze-thaw pipe bursts are the obvious missing one, plus seasonal rate adjustments and holiday guest occupancy) or trim title to '5 Common Causes.' (4) Add sources frontmatter and inline [n] citations to both files. (5) For summer specifically: the FAQ references also need citations since they repeat specific claims about tiered pricing and leakage.
confidence_basis: All EPA pages fetched directly from .gov domain (retrieved 2026-08-29). Exact quotes preserved for verification. Both target files read in full. Model sibling inspected for pattern compliance. Arithmetic verified by manual summation of table rows.
